title: What AI is, and what it isn't
essentialQuestion: How can you tell when a machine is using AI?
learningGoal: Explain how many AI tools make predictions from patterns in examples, and sort everyday tools into AI and not AI.

options: A tool that turns speech into typed words

sections.heading: Many AI tools learn from examples
sections.text: AI stands for artificial intelligence. Artificial means made by people. AI is a big field with many methods. Many AI systems used today learn patterns from data, and this lesson is about them. People give the program a lot of data, such as photos, sentences or voice recordings. The program looks for a pattern in the data. Then it uses that pattern to make a prediction. A prediction is a careful guess about something new, based on the patterns, not a random one. At Hillview Learning Centre, the translation tool learned from many sentences in two languages. When you type a sentence it has never seen, it predicts a good translation.
sections.simpler: AI means artificial intelligence. People make it. There are many kinds of AI. Many AI programs today learn from examples. This lesson is about them. People give a program lots of data, like photos or voices. It finds a pattern in the data. Then it makes a prediction. This is a careful guess about something new. It is not random. The Hillview translation tool learned from many sentences. It can guess how to translate a new one.

sections.heading: Not every machine uses AI
sections.text: Many machines are not AI. A calculator follows fixed steps that a person wrote, for sums with one right answer. It always gives 12 for 7 + 5, and it never learned that from examples. The bell at Hillview rings at nine o'clock because someone set a timer. The AI tools in this lesson are different, because they must estimate. A new voice or photo is never exactly like their examples. Still, following rules does not prove a tool is not AI. Some AI follows rules that people wrote, and some mixes rules and learning. A fan called “smart” might follow one simple rule, or it might learn. Sometimes the honest answer is “hard to say”.
sections.simpler: Many machines are not AI. A calculator follows steps a person wrote. It always says 7 + 5 is 12. It did not learn this. The Hillview bell rings at nine. Someone set a timer. The AI tools here must make a careful guess. A new photo is never the same as their examples. But some AI follows rules that people wrote. Some uses rules and examples. So it can be hard to tell. A “smart” fan may follow one rule, or it may learn.

sections.heading: AI is a tool, not a person
sections.text: AI can seem clever, but it does not think or feel like a person. It does not understand a photo or a sentence the way you do. It finds patterns in data and makes a guess. That guess can be wrong, especially when something is new or very different from its examples. People decide what an AI tool is for, what data it learns from and when to trust its answers. So you can ask three questions about any AI tool. What does it guess? What examples did it learn from? Who checks if it is right?
sections.simpler: AI can seem clever. But it does not think or feel like a person. It finds patterns and makes a guess. The guess can be wrong, more often when something is new. People choose what AI is for, its data and when to trust it. Ask three questions. What does it guess? What did it learn from? Who checks it?

glossary.definition: Computer systems that do tasks like seeing, talking or deciding. Many learn from examples.
glossary.example: The Hillview translation tool uses artificial intelligence.

glossary.definition: A set of steps that tells a computer what to do.
glossary.example: The calculator program follows the same steps every time.

glossary.definition: Facts, words, pictures or sounds that a computer can use.
glossary.example: The translation tool learned from data: many sentences in two languages.

glossary.definition: Something that happens again and again in a similar way.
glossary.example: The video site finds a pattern in what people watch.

glossary.definition: A careful guess, based on patterns, about something you do not know yet.
glossary.example: The translation is a prediction. It may not be right.

checks.question: Why does the Hillview translation tool count as AI?

options.text: It runs on the centre's shared laptop
options.feedback: Not quite. Many programs on a laptop are not AI. Look at how the translation tool learned.

options.text: It learned patterns from many examples
options.feedback: Yes. It learned from many sentences. Then it uses the pattern to guess a translation for a new one.

options.text: It gives the same answer every time
options.feedback: Not quite. Giving the same answer does not make a tool AI, or stop it being AI. Look at how the translation tool learned.

checks.question: The Hillview bell rings at nine o'clock every day. What is the best way to describe it?

options.text: It learned the time from examples
options.feedback: Not quite. Nobody gave the bell examples. Read about the bell in the second section.

options.text: It guesses when learners will arrive
options.feedback: Not quite. The bell does not guess. Read about the bell in the second section.

options.text: It follows a fixed step a person set
options.feedback: Yes. Someone set a timer. The bell does not learn from examples or estimate anything, so it is not AI.

One mistake it could make is ...
selfCheck: I said if it uses AI and gave a reason.
I named one mistake it could make or one thing a person should check.
write.example: I chose the voice typing tool. I think it uses AI because it has to make a careful guess at the words from each new voice. It learned from lots of voice recordings and found patterns in them. One mistake it could make is typing the wrong word when someone speaks fast or quietly. A person should check the typed words before using them. The calculator is different. It follows steps a person wrote, and it does not learn from examples.

speak.independentTask: Say out loud what AI is in two sentences. Then name one thing AI cannot do.

watch.title: What is Machine Learning?
watch.why: Two people who work with AI explain, in under three minutes, that most AI today learns patterns from examples.
watch.beforeQuestion: Where do you think AI is used every day?
watch.afterQuestion: How is machine learning different from a program that follows fixed steps?
watch.summary: In this short video, two people who work with AI talk about machine learning. AI is already part of everyday life. It helps choose what people see online, for example when they search. Many people imagine AI as a robot that thinks like a person. The speakers say that kind of AI is still many years away. Most AI today is machine learning. In the past, people had to write every step for a computer. With machine learning, people give the computer lots of examples. The computer finds patterns in the examples by itself. This is a bit like how you learn from practice. It is a new way to get computers to do useful jobs.
keyPoints: AI is already part of everyday tools, like internet searches.
The speakers say most AI today is machine learning: it finds patterns in examples.
People do not write every step. They give the computer examples.
watch.contentNote: The speakers name the companies they work for, and say that AI that thinks like a person is still decades away. That is their opinion, not a settled fact. Preview it first; learners can read the written summary instead.

educatorNotes: There is no single agreed line between AI and other programs (see the OECD source). AI is a broad field: Stanford HAI calls it computer systems that do tasks with human-like intelligence, and says modern AI often works by finding patterns in data. This lesson introduces that common modern kind (machine learning); rule-based AI, such as the expert systems in Lesson 2, is AI too. Accept “hard to say” and reward reasons, not the group a learner picks. The activity has no score.
Learners may not own a phone. Every tool in the list is one they might see at a centre or a shop, and the think question lets them pick a tool from the lesson.

The video is fast, native-speaker English and names real companies. The written summary covers the main idea. Someone on the team must still watch it before use (see content/courses/digital-world/README.md).
